title: Sugar on the cell surface isn't frosting — it's the brain's moat
dek: The mucins on brain endothelial cells are like a redwood forest; with aging the leaves fall off and the blood-brain barrier gets leaky. Restore the enzyme with gene therapy, and mice remember better.
why: A chemist explains how glycobiology unexpectedly opened the blood-brain barrier, with concrete mechanisms and numbers. The brain shuttle company in the second half is the most valuable part.
who: Founders and investors working on neurodegenerative disease, blood-brain barrier delivery, glycobiology, or biologics R&D; researchers interested in how basic science becomes a company.
skip: The first 10 minutes cover the history of glycobiology and the M&M analogy; fast-forward to the aging glycome discovery at 26:00.

points.h: Glycobiology was abandoned by its tools
points.body: In the 1960s and 70s, carbohydrates were taken as seriously as proteins, but once recombinant DNA arrived, proteins could be cloned, expressed, and studied — sugars could not. Sugars are not products of the central dogma; they are the result of enzymes encoded by hundreds of genes, and cannot be directly manipulated with molecular biology techniques. So the scientific world rushed to fields that could accelerate, and sugar science, technically difficult, was left behind. Bertozzi says this is not because sugars are unimportant, but because ‘not studying a field doesn't mean it's unimportant’.

points.h: She built the flashlight first, then talked biology
points.body: When she started her lab at Berkeley in 1996, sugar science lacked two things proteins had long had: sequencing (knowing which sugars exist) and live imaging (seeing where sugars are and how they move). Her lab's initial goal was to fill these two holes, and it took about a decade to develop bioorthogonal chemistry — a chemical reaction that can label sugars in living cells and has now become a general tool in life sciences. With a flashlight, you can see places no one had seen before.

points.h: No one had asked how sugars change with aging
points.body: Tony Wyss-Coray's lab was studying transcriptomic and proteomic changes in brain endothelial cells during aging — standard practice — but no one had asked about the glycome. A student who had rotated in Bertozzi's lab, Sophia, moved to Tony's lab and used sugar imaging reagents to compare the brain vasculature of old and young mice. The result was ‘absolutely striking’ — the changes in sugars were far more dramatic than any phenotype observed in the transcriptome or proteome.

points.h: Brain endothelial cells have redwood-like mucins
points.body: Mucins on the cell surface are like giant redwoods: tall, stiff, straight, towering above other structures. The mucin forest on brain endothelial cells is much thicker than in the blood vessels of the heart, kidney, or muscle, and is a landscape unique to the blood-brain barrier. With aging, this forest becomes like winter — leaves gone, trees bare, you can see through; young mice are like spring, with dense foliage. Sophia found that the enzymes responsible for synthesizing these sugars decrease in abundance in old mice. Using a gene therapy vector to restore the enzymes, the mucins recovered, blood-brain barrier leakage decreased, and mice navigated mazes faster.

points.h: A reagent crossed the blood-brain barrier on its own
points.body: Sophia injected a mucin-binding reagent into mice and found that within hours it first bound to blood vessels, then crossed the blood-brain barrier on its own into the brain parenchyma. Textbooks say proteins cannot cross the blood-brain barrier alone, which is also the biggest pain point for biologics companies making brain drugs. This accidental discovery made the team realize it could be used as a brain shuttle to deliver cargo into the brain. Sophia now has her own lab at Harvard, and she, Bertozzi, Tony, and another student are spinning out a company to do brain shuttling.

More than 150 biologics have been approved for immune diseases, a similar number for cancer, but only 15 for central nervous system diseases, and most are given by intrathecal injection — a lumbar puncture, invasive, takes a whole day, and is hard to scale. If these drugs could be converted to ordinary intravenous injection, it would be transformative for patients. Drug types that can enter the brain include monoclonal antibodies, enzyme replacement therapies, siRNA and antisense oligonucleotides, mRNA lipid nanoparticles, and viral and non-viral gene therapy vectors.

points.h: CD22 is the brake on the brain's immune cells
points.body: Tony's lab found that in microglia of aged and Alzheimer's disease mice, the sugar-binding receptor CD22 (Siglec-2) is upregulated. Bertozzi's lab had previously studied this receptor family in cancer: when upregulated, they inhibit immune cells, allowing cancer cells to grow unchecked. Microglia are the brain's scavengers, responsible for eating protein aggregates, and their dysfunction is linked to neurodegenerative diseases. Blocking CD22 with antibodies made microglia in aged mice more active and the brain cleaner. But at the time there was no brain shuttle, so only intracranial injection was possible, making human therapy impossible; now with shuttle technology, this antibody can be revisited.

points.h: Today's drugs are built on century-old chemistry
points.body: Bioorthogonal chemistry was developed in the early 2000s and has now been integrated into the toolkit of chemists and biologists; there are approved drugs that use this chemistry. But in her Nobel lecture, Bertozzi traced back and found that the basic chemistry they used to develop these reactions was published in 1915, 1919, and 1950 (from Germany) — all old German-language journals that needed translation. Those chemists could not have foreseen that a hundred years later someone would use it to make cancer drugs. She says most scientists will not know the true impact of their work in their lifetime, and we must invest in basic science without knowing the impact or timeline, otherwise the entire pipeline will eventually dry up.

terms.def: Chemical reactions that can be performed in living cells without interfering with natural biological processes, used to label and image molecules such as sugars.
The entire collection of glycans on the cell surface, analogous to the genome or proteome.
Highly glycosylated cell surface proteins with a bottlebrush-like structure that form a thick layer on brain endothelial cells.
An inhibitory receptor that binds sialic acid, suppresses immune cells in cancer, and is upregulated in microglia with aging.
A molecular carrier that can deliver biologic cargo across the blood-brain barrier into the brain.
